Skill content (for context on what the skill does):
<skill_content>
---
name: fetching-bilibili-video-data
description: Fetch real, live Bilibili (B站) video stats — view/like/coin/favorite/share/reply counts, uploader name and follower count, and time-synced danmaku (弹幕) — from Bilibili's API instead of estimating or recalling numbers from memory. Accepts a full bilibili.com URL, a bare BVID, an old-style av number, or a b23.tv short link. Use when the user pastes a Bilibili video link or ID, asks for a video's views/likes/coins/favorites/shares/replies/danmaku, wants to know how a B站 video performed or how its audience reacted, is drafting an analysis piece citing B站 numbers, or asks anything that would otherwise require guessing a Bilibili statistic. Also use to check an uploader's (UP主) follower count, or to get a video's subtitles (ask for the user's own login cookie first — never fetch subtitles silently). Never estimate, round, or recall a Bilibili number from memory — always fetch it live, and say plainly when a number can't be retrieved instead of presenting a guess as fact.
compatibility: Works anywhere Python 3.8+ and outbound HTTPS access to api.bilibili.com, comment.bilibili.com, and b23.tv are available. No authentication needed for view/like/coin/favorite/share/reply/danmaku/follower data. Subtitle *content* download needs the user's own Bilibili SESSDATA cookie, supplied only after asking. Stdlib-only Python (urllib, json, xml.etree) — no packages to install.
---

# Fetching Bilibili Video Data

Bilibili view/like/coin/favorite counts change by the second, and there is no way to
recover a real number for a specific video from training data — any number produced
without a live fetch is a guess wearing the shape of a fact. This skill exists so that
never happens: it calls Bilibili's own public API and reports exactly what comes back,
including when part of it can't be retrieved.

## The one rule everything below serves

**Never hand-type, round, or recall a Bilibili number.** Every statistic in your final
answer must trace back to a field in `scripts/bilibili_fetch.py`'s JSON output for this
specific run. If a field is `null` or the run produced a warning about it, say so
explicitly — "reply count wasn't available because..." — rather than filling the gap
with something plausible-sounding. A wrong number presented with confidence is worse
than no number, especially in anything the user intends to cite.

## Step 1: Run the fetch script

Whatever form the user pasted — a full URL, a bare BVID (`BV...`), an old-style av
number (`av123456`), or a `b23.tv` short link — pass it straight through as-is. The
script does the parsing:

```bash
python3 scripts/bilibili_fetch.py "<whatever the user pasted>"
```

This is a fixed procedure, not something to reimplement inline: resolving a short link,
handling both ID schemes, and decoding the danmaku endpoint's response each have a
specific correct way to do them (see `references/api-notes.md` if you need to know why),
and getting any of them wrong produces either a crash or, worse, data that looks right
but silently isn't. Run the script; don't hand-roll the HTTP calls yourself.

The script prints one JSON object to stdout and exits non-zero if it couldn't resolve
the input or the video doesn't exist — check the exit code and the `errors` array before
treating anything as data. A partial success (core stats present, danmaku or subtitles
warned-off) still exits 0; read the `warnings` array in that case and carry those
caveats into your answer.

Useful flags:
- `--no-danmaku` — skip the danmaku fetch if the user only wants the numbers
- `--danmaku-limit N` — cap how many danmaku entries come back (default 2000; the
  underlying endpoint itself caps out well before "every comment ever posted" on
  high-volume videos regardless of this flag — see below)

## Step 2: Report what actually came back

Present the fields from `video` and `uploader` as the real, current numbers they are —
attach the `fetched_at` timestamp when the user is using this for anything they'd cite,
since "as of when" matters as much as the number itself for a fast-moving stat.

For danmaku, don't just count them — read through the `text` fields as the qualitative
signal the user actually asked for. Danmaku are time-synced audience reactions, not a
generic comment section: a cluster of the same phrase at one timestamp usually means a
specific moment in the video (a plot twist, a punchline, a claim viewers are disputing)
provoked a shared reaction. Group by theme or by timestamp cluster when summarizing,
don't just list them.

**If `stat.danmaku` (the official reported total) is larger than the number of entries
actually returned**, the script already added a warning about this — relay it. The
legacy danmaku endpoint this script uses returns a capped snapshot, not guaranteed-complete
history, for videos with a lot of danmaku. Treat what you got as a representative sample
of audience reaction, not an exhaustive transcript, and say so if the user is drawing a
quantitative conclusion from it (e.g. "80% of danmaku mention X" is not a claim this data
supports unless you've confirmed you have the complete set).

## Step 3: Subtitles — ask before fetching

The script always lists *available* subtitle tracks (`subtitles.available`) without
needing login. It does **not** download subtitle content unless you pass
`--fetch-subtitles`, and content for some videos additionally needs the user's own
Bilibili session (`--sessdata`).

If `subtitles.available` is non-empty and the user hasn't already asked for subtitles
specifically:
1. Mention that subtitle tracks exist and ask if they want them.
2. If yes, ask the user to provide their Bilibili `SESSDATA` cookie value (from their
   own logged-in browser session — walk them through finding it in dev tools if needed).
   Never ask for or handle their Bilibili password; the cookie is the only credential
   this needs, and even that should come from the user, not be guessed or reused from
   anywhere else.
3. Rerun with `--fetch-subtitles --sessdata <value>`.

Don't fetch subtitle content silently even if a `SESSDATA` happens to be available from
earlier in the conversation — the user asking for it each time is the point, not a
formality to route around.

## Step 4: Report failures as failures

If the script exits non-zero, its `errors` array explains why (video not found, deleted,
region/age-gated, or a malformed ID). Relay that to the user plainly and stop — don't
retry with a guessed alternate ID, and don't fall back to describing what the video
"probably" looks like based on its title or URL. "I couldn't fetch this — Bilibili
returned: `<error>`" is a complete and correct answer; a fabricated substitute is not.

## Reference

`references/api-notes.md` — which Bilibili endpoints this script calls, why each ID
form is handled the way it is, and the known limitation on danmaku completeness in more
detail. Read it if you need to explain a failure mode to the user beyond what the
script's own error message says, or if you're extending the script.

---

Lifecycle: capability-uplift, timelessness 9/10, last verified against claude-sonnet-5
(2026-08). The gap this skill fills — a model has no way to know a specific video's
current view count from training data, because that number changes continuously — is
structural, not a training-data or reasoning limitation that a future model closes on
its own; a smarter model still cannot fetch live data it wasn't given a tool to fetch.
It scores 9 rather than 10 because Bilibili's own API surface (endpoint paths, response
shapes, the danmaku endpoint's cap) can change independently of model capability and is
the part most likely to need a re-check over time.
